label: Drinking out
rationale: A night out drinking: the invitation, asking about smoking, and whether you can hold your drink.
mixUps: nomi ni iku is the drinking version of gohan ni iku, and nomi means alcohol without saying osake. osake ga tsuyoi and osake ga yowai describe the drinker, while kono osake tsuyoi means the drink is strong. Tobacco takes suu, not nomu.

targets.verbSense: go; with a verb stem or activity noun + ni, go (out) to do it (tabe ni iku, kaimono ni iku)
targets.use: The standard invitation and plan for a night out: kondo nomi ni ikou (let's go for a drink sometime), kyou nomi ni ikanai? Bare nomi already means alcohol. Naming the drink is fine too (osake nomi ni iku, koohii nomi ni iku), and a café break is ocha shi ni iku. Casual speech sometimes drops ni (nomi iku).
targets.notes: A drinking party with colleagues or a club is a nomikai, and moving on to a second place afterwards is the nijikai (second round).

example.romaji: kondo, issho ni nomi ni ikou yo.
example.ja: 今度、一緒に飲みに行こうよ。
example.english: Let's go for a drink together sometime.

examplePolite.romaji: kondo, issho ni nomi ni ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 今度、一緒に飲みに行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's go for a drink together sometime.

targets.trap: Dictionaries give kitsuen suru for 'smoke', but that is the word on signs and forms (kitsuenjo, kin'en); in speech you inhale the tobacco: tabako (o) suu. kemuri names only the smoke itself.
targets.use: Used to ask about smoking and to say whether you smoke: tabako suu? (do you smoke?), sutte mo ii? (mind if I smoke?). Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: Restaurants ask kitsuen seki ka kin'en seki (smoking or non-smoking seat?); kin'en on a sign means no smoking. tabako o nomu is dated (older speakers); don't use it.

examplePolite.romaji: tabako o sutte mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: タバコを吸ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Do you mind if I smoke?

targets.verbSense: weak, having little strength or tolerance
targets.trap: English has no set phrase here, so learners fall back on amari nomenai (fine, but blunt). Japanese says the drinker is weak: osake ga yowai (or osake ni yowai). Careful: kono osake tsuyoi is about the drink (high proof), not the drinker.
partners: asa (mornings: asa ga yowai, not a morning person)
i (stomach: i ga yowai, a delicate stomach)
targets.use: Said about yourself to turn down drinks gently (osake yowai n desu) or about someone who gets drunk fast. Casual speech drops ga.
targets.notes: osake ni yowai is equally fine; osake ga tsuyoi is the opposite. With conditions only ni works: samusa ni yowai (can't take the cold), atsusa ni yowai (can't take the heat), norimono ni yowai (get travel-sick); samusa ga yowai would mean the cold is mild.

example.romaji: osake yowai kara, ippai dake ni shitoku.
example.ja: お酒弱いから、一杯だけにしとく。
example.english: I'm a lightweight, so I'll just have one.

examplePolite.romaji: osake yowai n de, ippai dake ni shitokimasu.
examplePolite.ja: お酒弱いんで、一杯だけにしときます。
examplePolite.english: I'm not much of a drinker, so I'll just have the one.

targets.verbSense: strong; with something you take or face, able to handle it
partners: kikai (machines: kikai ni tsuyoi, good with tech)
targets.use: Said about people at drinking parties, often as surprised praise: osake tsuyoi ne! (you can really drink!), or as a question, osake tsuyoi n desu ka? Casual speech drops ga, and osake ni tsuyoi is equally common.
targets.notes: osake ga yowai is the opposite. With the drink as the subject, kono osake tsuyoi means the drink is high-proof. Someone who never seems to get drunk is jokingly called a zaru (a sieve).

example.romaji: osake tsuyoi ne. zenzen kao ni denai.
example.ja: お酒強いね。全然顔に出ない。
example.english: You can really drink. It doesn't even show on your face.

examplePolite.romaji: osake ga tsuyoi desu ne. zenzen kao ni demasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: お酒が強いですね。全然顔に出ませんね。
examplePolite.english: You can really drink. It doesn't show on your face at all.

reviewPool.english: suit someone, look good on someone
not suit someone, can't make it (a time)
